whole downfield passing game for one snap: the quarterback has one place to throw. When the screen is
sniffed out, the quarterback's best play is usually to throw the ball into the ground at the back's feet. That
is legal, because the back is an eligible receiver right there ([intentional grounding](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding),
the foul for throwing the ball away under pressure, applies only to a pass that is not in the direction and
vicinity of an eligible receiver), and an incompletion is much better than a sack or a tipped
interception.[^grounding]

(For the stat sheet: a screen thrown forward, even from behind the line, is an ordinary pass, with an attempt,
passing yards and receiving yards, which is how this chapter's play-by-play data can count screens at all. One
thrown *backward* is a lateral, as [The Quick Game](04-03-quick-game.qmd) showed.)

### Swing and flare: not screens

Casual viewers call any short pass to a running back a screen. Most of them are not, and the difference
tells you what the offense was thinking.

```{python}
#| label: fig-swing-vs-screen
#| fig-cap: "Swing route or screen? Same formation, same defense, two different plays. Left, a swing route: the linemen stay in pass protection, nobody releases, and the back leaves at the snap, bows backward and out toward the sideline and catches the ball on the move, with the safety over the slot coming to meet him (dashed orange). He has to beat that man himself. Right, the slow screen of the figure above: the back first sets as if to block, the left side of the line releases in front of him, and when he catches it he has three blockers between him and the defense."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.4))
for ax, screen in zip(axes, (False, True)):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if screen:
        slow_screen(p)
    else:
        pass_set(p)
        p.dropback(1.6)
        p.route("RB", r.swing(9.0), side=-1)
        go_to(p, "RB", (6.0, -11.5), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(1.0, -11.0)])
        go_to(p, "H", (14.0, -9.0), "route")
        go_to(p, "X", (16.0, -15.5), "route")
        p._compile()
        t_c = float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][0])
        throw_at(p, "RB", t_c)
    fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-19.5, 11.0), window=(-11.5, 17.5))
    if screen:
        say(fld, p, 10.6, -6.4, "three linemen\nin front", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        te = [e[2] for e in p.ball_events if e[0] == "pass"][0]
        say(fld, p, -10.0, 4.6, f"ball out\nat ~{te:.1f} s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -9.2, -12.4, "R: blocks a count,\nthen settles in", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Slow screen: blockers out front")
    else:
        q = p.players["SS"]
        branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), (1.6, -11.0)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.5)
        say(fld, p, -3.4, 4.6, "the line keeps\npass-blocking", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -9.6, -12.0, "R leaves at the snap;\ncaught on the move", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 4.6, -15.6, "SS comes\nto meet him", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Swing route: no blockers")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

A [**swing route**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-swing-route) is a running back's route that bows
backward and then out toward the sideline, so he catches the ball on the move behind or at the line.
A [**flare**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flare) is a quicker, flatter release toward the sideline that
bends slightly upfield; many playbooks use the two words for the same thing. Either way, it is a pass
*route*: the line keeps blocking and nobody releases in front of the back.
Its purposes are different from a screen's. It is an outlet when the downfield routes are covered (a
[checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown) the quarterback can always find), a way to pull a
linebacker wide and open the middle for another route, and a way to get a fast back the ball in space against
a slower linebacker.

The tell on a broadcast is the offensive line. **If linemen leave their rushers and slide out to one side
before the ball is thrown, it is a screen** (or a run). If the line is still pass-blocking when the back catches
it, it was a route. The second tell is the back's first steps. A swing back leaves at the snap and runs his path.
A screen back *waits*: he sets as if to block, then slips out and settles behind the released linemen. Don't rely
on timing: a swing can be thrown at once or late as a checkdown.

## The screen family

Once you see the slow screen's logic (let the rush come, release the linemen, throw behind them), the rest of
the family is variations on who catches it and where the blockers go.

### Tunnel and jailbreak: screens to a wide receiver

```{python}
#| label: fig-tunnel-jailbreak
#| fig-cap: "Two wide receiver screens that use the offensive line. Left, a tunnel screen to Z: Z takes two hard steps upfield to back his cornerback off, then comes back inside toward the ball and catches it behind the line. The Y (an eligible receiver, so he may go downfield) blocks out on the cornerback; the RT and RG show a quick pass set, release outward along the line, and climb to the nickel and the Mike once the ball is thrown (dashed); Z runs up the 'tunnel' between them. Right, a jailbreak screen to H: at the snap the LT, LG and C skip pass protection entirely and sprint out flat to the left, while H takes two steps upfield and comes back behind the line for the throw; the linemen turn upfield to block only after it (dashed). The two rushers they would have blocked are left free (ringed). X blocks his cornerback."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 3.25))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("tunnel", "jail")):
    p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
    if kind == "tunnel":
        for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
        # a quick pass set, then out along the line; they climb only once the ball is thrown (dashed)
        go_to(p, "RT", (0.6, 7.4), "block", via=[(-1.0, 4.2)], speed=5.0)
        go_to(p, "RG", (0.6, 4.2), "block", via=[(-0.9, 2.4)], speed=4.5)
        go_to(p, "Y", (4.4, 14.0), "block", speed=4.5)                          # an eligible: may go downfield
        go_to(p, "Z", (-0.8, 11.2), "route", via=[(3.0, 15.4)], speed=5.5)     # sell upfield, come back inside
        go_to(p, "Z", (11.0, 10.6), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(3.0, 10.4)])
        p._compile()
        te = throw_at(p, "Z", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "Z" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        p.path("QB", [(-0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "SDE", (-3.6, 4.4), "rush", speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "SDT", (-3.4, 1.4), "rush", speed=3.4)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.8, 20.5), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
        for k, end in (("NB", (3.4, 8.2)), ("MIKE", (3.8, 4.4)), ("RCB", (7.6, 15.0))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "RT", (2.6, 8.0))
        after_throw(fld, p, "RG", (3.0, 4.4))
        say(fld, p, 9.0, 13.4, "the tunnel", color=GREEN, fontsize=7, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -5.6, 12.0, "Z: two steps up,\nthen back inside", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, -6.4, 4.6, f"ball out at ~{te:.1f} s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Tunnel screen")
    else:
        # the screen-side linemen never pass-set: they sprint out along the line at the snap
        go_to(p, "LT", (0.6, -12.0), "block", via=[(-0.4, -6.2)], speed=5.5)
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.6, -8.4), "block", via=[(-0.4, -4.2)], speed=5.5)
        go_to(p, "C", (0.5, -4.6), "block", via=[(-0.3, -1.6)], speed=5.0)
        for k in ("RG", "RT"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
        go_to(p, "H", (2.0, -9.4), "route", speed=6.0)                          # a two-step stem upfield ...
        go_to(p, "H", (-1.8, -10.4), "route", speed=4.0)                        # ... then back behind the line
        go_to(p, "H", (10.0, -10.6), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(2.0, -10.2)])
        p._compile()
        te = throw_at(p, "H", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "H" and a.kind == "route"][-1]) + 0.05)
        go_to(p, "X", (3.0, -15.4), "block", speed=4.0)
        p.path("QB", [(-0.8, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        for k, end in (("WDE", (-3.8, -2.2)), ("WDT", (-3.8, -0.4))):
            go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=4.5)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-20.5, 6.8), window=(-9.0, 15.0))
        for k in ("WDE", "WDT"):
            q = p.players[k]
            ring(fld, p, q.d, q.w, r_=1.2)
        for k, end in (("SS", (3.6, -12.4)), ("WILL", (4.0, -8.6)), ("MIKE", (4.4, -4.8))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "LT", (2.6, -12.2))
        after_throw(fld, p, "LG", (3.0, -8.6))
        after_throw(fld, p, "C", (3.4, -4.8))
        say(fld, p, 9.4, -5.4, "linemen sprint out\nat the snap, flat", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.8, weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -7.0, -6.0, "rushers\nleft free", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
        say(fld, p, -6.6, -14.6, f"ball out at ~{te:.1f} s", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Jailbreak screen")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6, rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
legend(fig, ["block", "after", "run", "pass", "react"], ncol=5, y=0.06)
plt.show()
```

A [**tunnel screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tunnel-screen) goes to an outside receiver who
comes back *inside*, toward the ball. The receiver's first steps upfield matter: the cornerback, seeing a
receiver attack him, backs up, and that cushion is the space the receiver catches the ball in. Two linemen
show a quick pass set, then release outward along the line to wall off the defenders inside, and a teammate
(here the Y, a tight end in the slot, a natural blocker) blocks the cornerback from the outside. The receiver
catches it in the gap between them and runs up the "tunnel."

A [**jailbreak screen**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-jailbreak-screen) gets its name from what the line
does: at the snap, the linemen on the screen side do not pass-block at all, they break out and sprint toward
the screen side, leaving their rushers free. That makes it a *quick* screen, thrown in about a second, because
nobody is blocking those rushers. Its advantage over the now and bubble screens of 04-03 is size: instead of a
receiver trying to block a defender, a 310-pound lineman arrives in space against a 190-pound cornerback.

Both screens obey the one-yard rule the same way the slow screen does. The linemen sprint *sideways*, along the
line, and the ball comes out about a second after the snap, so they are barely a yard past the line when it is
thrown; only then do they turn upfield onto the linebackers and safeties. That is why the receiver's two steps
upfield matter on both: they buy the second the linemen need to get across.

| | Tunnel screen | Jailbreak screen |
|---|---|---|
| Who catches it | An outside receiver | Usually a slot receiver (here H) |
| His path | Two steps upfield, then back *inside* between blockers | A step or two up, then back behind the line |
| The linemen | Two or three show a quick pass set, then release outward | The screen-side linemen sprint out at the snap: no pass set at all |
| Who blocks the corner | A teammate outside him (here the Y) | A teammate outside him (here X) |
| Ball out | About a second | About a second |

: The two wide receiver screens side by side, as this book names them. {#tbl-tunnel-jailbreak}

Playbook names in this family vary a lot. Some teams call the tunnel screen a jailbreak, and some call any
screen with the whole line releasing a "jailbreak." The features in @tbl-tunnel-jailbreak are what matter: who
catches it, which way he runs, and whether the linemen sell pass first.

### Tight end and middle screens

```{python}
#| label: fig-te-middle
#| fig-cap: "Two more members of the family (receivers not involved in the play stand still). Left, a tight end screen: the Y blocks the end for a count, then slides out to the right flat behind the line; the RG and RT set, release outward along the line and, once the ball is thrown, climb to the Mike and the nickel (dashed); Z runs his cornerback off. Right, a middle screen to the back: the tackles push the ends wide and past the quarterback; the guards and center set, let the defensive tackles through, and form a wall at the line in front of the back, climbing to the linebackers only once the ball is thrown (dashed); the back slips into the middle behind the rushers, in the space they left."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.1))
for ax, kind in zip(axes, ("te", "mid")):
    if kind == "te":
        p = Play(spread(y_inline=True), nickel(extra={"NB": (5.0, 8.4), "RCB": (7.0, 15.0)}), los=35, to_go=None)
        for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
            p.block(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
        # set for a count, then out along the line (dashed: the climb after the throw)
        go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, 3.6), "block", via=[(-1.6, 1.8)], speed=2.4)
        go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 7.0), "block", via=[(-1.6, 3.4)], speed=2.4)
        go_to(p, "Y", (-1.0, 5.2), "block", speed=0.8)                          # block the end for a count ...
        go_to(p, "Y", (-2.4, 8.4), "route", delay=0.2, speed=3.5)               # ... then slide out
        go_to(p, "Y", (9.0, 10.4), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(1.0, 9.6)])
        go_to(p, "Z", (14.0, 14.5), "route")
        go_to(p, "QB", (-8.8, -0.4), speed=2.2)
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "Y", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "Y" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        go_to(p, "SDE", (-5.4, 2.6), "rush", speed=3.4)
        go_to(p, "SDT", (-5.0, 1.0), "rush", speed=3.4)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-6.8, 18.5), window=(-11.0, 15.5))
        for k, end in (("NB", (3.2, 7.8)), ("MIKE", (3.6, 3.8)), ("RCB", (11.0, 15.0))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), end], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "RG", (2.4, 3.8))
        after_throw(fld, p, "RT", (2.2, 7.8))
        say(fld, p, -6.6, 11.8, "Y: block a count,\nthen slide out", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Tight end screen")
    else:
        p = Play(spread(), nickel(), los=35, to_go=None)
        go_to(p, "LT", (-3.2, -5.0), "block", speed=2.6)                         # push the ends wide
        go_to(p, "RT", (-3.2, 5.0), "block", speed=2.6)
        # set, let the tackles through, then shuffle up to the line in front of the catch (dashed: after the throw)
        go_to(p, "LG", (0.5, -2.2), "block", via=[(-1.7, -1.6)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "C", (0.5, 0.2), "block", via=[(-1.7, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, 2.6), "block", via=[(-1.7, 1.6)], speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -1.6), speed=2.0)
        go_to(p, "RB", (-2.6, -0.4), "route", delay=0.7, speed=2.5)
        go_to(p, "RB", (9.0, -0.3), "run", delay=0.1)
        go_to(p, "QB", (-9.0, 0.6), speed=2.2)
        p._compile()
        throw_at(p, "RB", float([a.t1 for a in p.actions if a.key == "RB" and a.kind == "route"][0]) + 0.05)
        for k, end in (("WDE", (-4.4, -6.2)), ("SDE", (-4.4, 6.2)), ("WDT", (-7.2, -1.4)), ("SDT", (-7.2, 2.0))):
            go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.6)
        fld = draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-12.5, 12.5), window=(-11.0, 15.5))
        for k, end in (("WILL", (3.8, -2.6)), ("MIKE", (4.0, 1.8))):
            q = p.players[k]
            branch(fld, p, [(q.d, q.w), (q.d + 2.0, q.w)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3)
        after_throw(fld, p, "LG", (5.4, -2.6))
        after_throw(fld, p, "C", (5.6, 1.6))
        after_throw(fld, p, "RG", (3.6, 5.6))
        say(fld, p, -9.6, -8.0, "tackles push\nthe ends wide", color=style.OFFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        say(fld, p, 10.6, 6.4, "G, C, G: a wall at the\nline, then up to the LBs", color=GREEN, fontsize=6.6,
            weight="bold")
        say(fld, p, -9.4, 6.4, "DTs let\nthrough", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.6)
        panel_title(ax, "Middle screen")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6, rect=(0, 0.06, 1, 1))
legend(fig, ["block", "after", "run", "pass", "react"], ncol=5, y=0.06)
plt.show()
```

The **tight end screen** is the slow screen run with a tight end: he blocks the end for a count, which
is exactly what defenders expect a tight end to do, then slides out behind the line on his side. It is a
good call against defenses that bring the edge rusher hard, because the rusher is the man the tight end just
let go. The **middle screen** puts the back in the middle of the field instead of the flat. The tackles
push the ends wide, as they do on any dropback; the guards and center let the defensive tackles through, set up
a wall at the line, and climb to the linebackers as the ball is thrown; the back slips into the space the
defensive tackles just left.
It punishes interior pass rushers who get upfield fast, and linebackers who drop deep on passing downs.

::: {.callout-important title="Why screens exist"}
Every good pass rush has the same weakness: its rushers are trying to get *upfield* as fast as possible,
toward the quarterback. A screen uses that against them. It turns the rushers' speed into distance from the
ball, and it turns the five biggest people on the field, who are usually stuck at the line, into blockers in
open space. The price is that a screen gives up the rest of the passing game for one snap, needs precise
timing from seven or more players, and turns into a loss, or worse, if the defense recognizes it.
:::

## Screens punish pressure

The logic of the screen predicts something you can check: **screens should get better the more defenders
rush.** Every extra rusher is one more defender running away from the ball, and one fewer defender in front
of it.

Watch it against a six-man blitz. In @fig-screen-blitz the defense shows pressure before the snap: both
linebackers walk up into the gaps beside the center (a [double A-gap mug](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-a-gap-mug),
built in [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd)), and behind them the
defensive backs play man coverage. The free safety has come down to about eight yards to cover the running
back man-to-man, so nobody is left deep. Six rushers, five protectors plus the back.

```{python}
#| label: fig-screen-blitz
#| fig-cap: "The slow screen against a six-man blitz, frame by frame (simulated, BDB-format). (1) Six defenders show blitz; the Mike and Will (ringed) stand in the A gaps. (2) The LT, LG and C let their men go and release left along the line; the back (ringed), who appeared to pick up a blitzer, slides out behind them. (3) Four rushers converge on the quarterback, who throws over them. (4) The ball is out, so the linemen have turned upfield in front of the back, and the only defender left to beat is the free safety (ringed), the man assigned to cover him. Every blitzer is behind the play."
def screen_vs_blitz():
    dfn = nickel(extra={"MIKE": (1.5, 0.8), "WILL": (1.5, -0.8), "WDT": (1.0, -2.6), "LCB": (6.0, -15.5),
                        "RCB": (6.0, 15.5)},
                 shell="zero")
    p = Play(spread(), dfn, los=35, to_go=8)
    for k in ("RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=1.5)
    go_to(p, "LT", (-1.4, -3.4), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LT", (0.8, -9.8), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0)     # flat release: within a yard at the throw
    go_to(p, "LG", (-1.4, -1.8), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "LG", (0.8, -4.6), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "C", (-1.3, 0.0), "block", speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "C", (0.6, -6.2), "block", delay=0.45, speed=5.0, via=[(-0.4, -4.4)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.2, -2.0), speed=2.0)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-3.0, -7.4), "route", delay=0.35, speed=3.4, via=[(-4.4, -4.6)])
    go_to(p, "RB", (9.0, -9.0), "run", speed=6.0, via=[(-1.5, -8.0), (3.0, -8.0)])
    go_to(p, "QB", (-8.6, 0.2), speed=2.6)
    go_to(p, "QB", (-10.4, 0.8), speed=1.6)
    p.pass_to("RB", t=2.0)
    go_to(p, "X", (15.0, -15.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "H", (5.0, -9.4), "route")
    go_to(p, "Y", (8.0, 9.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "Z", (12.0, 15.0), "route")
    # the rush: the screen side lets them through; they converge on the quarterback
    go_to(p, "WILL", (-7.6, -3.2), "rush", speed=4.4, via=[(-1.0, -0.5)])
    go_to(p, "MIKE", (-7.4, 2.4), "rush", speed=4.2, via=[(-1.0, 0.1)])
    go_to(p, "WDT", (-9.0, -0.8), "rush", speed=4.4, via=[(-1.0, -2.4)])
    go_to(p, "WDE", (-6.4, -4.6), "rush", speed=4.2, via=[(-1.6, -4.6)])
    go_to(p, "SDT", (-0.4, 2.0), speed=1.2)
    go_to(p, "SDE", (-0.6, 4.4), speed=1.2)
    # man coverage: each defender runs with his receiver; the free safety has the back
    go_to(p, "LCB", (15.0, -15.0), speed=6.5)
    go_to(p, "SS", (6.0, -9.0), speed=5.0)
    go_to(p, "NB", (9.0, 8.5), speed=6.0)
    go_to(p, "RCB", (12.5, 14.5), speed=5.5)
    go_to(p, "FS", (5.0, -5.0), speed=1.6)
    go_to(p, "FS", (4.6, -8.0), speed=5.0)
    # once the ball is out (2.0 s) the released linemen turn upfield (rule 8-3-2 lets them advance now)
    kf, _, _ = p._compile()
    for k, end in (("LT", (4.4, -10.6)), ("LG", (3.6, -6.8)), ("C", (3.0, -8.6))):
        go_to(p, k, end, "block", delay=max(0.0, 2.05 - float(kf[k][-1, 0])), speed=4.5)
    return p


sp = screen_vs_blitz()
play_movie(sp, [0.0, 0.9, 2.0, 3.0],
           notes=["six show blitz: the Mike and\nWill stand in the A gaps",
                  "LT, LG, C let them go and\nrelease; the back slides out",
                  "four rushers converge;\nthe throw goes over them",
                  "linemen turn upfield in front\nof him; every blitzer is behind"],
           frame_rings=[(("MIKE", style.DEFENSE), ("WILL", style.DEFENSE)),
                        (("RB", style.THIRD),), (("RB", style.THIRD),), (("RB", style.THIRD), ("FS", style.DEFENSE))],
           lateral=(-20.0, 8.0), window=(-11.8, 10.6), throw_t=2.0)
```

The data agrees, strikingly. FTN's charters count the pass rushers on every dropback, so we can split
pass attempts by how many came after the quarterback.

```{python}
#| label: fig-screen-rushers
#| fig-cap: "Screens get better as the rush gets bigger. EPA per pass attempt by the number of pass rushers, 2022-2025 regular seasons: screens of every kind (blue), running back screens alone (green) and every other pass (orange). Against three rushers (with eight defenders in coverage), screens are among the worst plays in football; against six or more, they beat ordinary passes. The six-plus group is small (labelled counts), so read its exact height loosely and its direction firmly. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 3.7))
xs = [3, 4, 5, 6]
lab = {3: "3", 4: "4", 5: "5", 6: "6+"}
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
series = [("Other passes", SCR[~SCR["screen"]].set_index("rushers"), style.SERIES[1]),
          ("All screens", SCR[SCR["screen"]].set_index("rushers"), style.SERIES[0]),
          ("RB screens", RBS, style.SERIES[2])]
for name, df, col in series:
    df = df.reindex(xs)
    ax.plot(xs, df["epa"], color=col, marker="o", ms=6, mec=style.SURFACE, mew=1.2, lw=2, zorder=3)
    ax.annotate(name, (6, df["epa"].iloc[-1]), xytext=(8, 0), textcoords="offset points", va="center",
                fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK_2)
    if name != "Other passes":
        for x_, (n_, e_) in zip(xs, zip(df["n"], df["epa"])):
            off = (0, -12) if name == "All screens" else ((-20, -2) if x_ == 4 else (0, 8))
            ax.annotate(f"n={int(n_):,}", (x_, e_), xytext=off, textcoords="offset points", ha="center",
                        fontsize=6.3, color=style.MUTED)
ax.set_xticks(xs, [lab[x] for x in xs])
ax.set_xlim(2.7, 6.9)
ax.set_ylim(-0.25, 0.2)
ax.set_xlabel("Pass rushers on the play", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per pass attempt", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.set_title("The more they rush, the better the screen", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Read @fig-screen-rushers from left to right. Against a three-man rush, all screens averaged
`{python} f"{SCR.set_index(['screen', 'rushers']).loc[(True, 3), 'epa']:+.2f}"` EPA per attempt: the defense
has eight players in coverage and no rushers to fool, so the screen is just a short pass into a crowd.
Against six or more rushers they averaged `{python} f"{SCR.set_index(['screen', 'rushers']).loc[(True, 6), 'epa']:+.2f}"`,
better than other passes against the same pressure. Running back screens, the purest version of the idea,
climb the most steeply.

Coverage matters too. Against man coverage, the defender assigned to the back (usually a linebacker or, as in
@fig-screen-blitz, a safety) has to chase him, which means running straight into the released linemen. That is
why screens pair so well against [Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0) blitzes (man coverage with
nobody deep, as in @fig-screen-blitz) and Cover 1 blitzes. Against zone, the danger is an underneath defender
who simply sits in the flat where the screen is going and waits for it.

Two cautions about the chart. First, selection: offenses call screens when they *expect* pressure, and a screen called into a
blitz is likely to be the right call at the right moment, so these averages flatter screens a little. Second,
the typical screen is not a great play: across all rush counts, screens averaged
`{python} f"{LG_SCREEN_EPA:+.2f}"` EPA per attempt, below ordinary passes. Screens are not an engine of an
offense. They are a **tax on pressure**: a play that makes blitzing expensive, so that the defense rushes four
more often, which helps every other pass the offense throws. Screens made up about
`{python} pct(SCREEN_SHARE.loc[2025])` of pass attempts in 2025, and `{python} pct(SCR_RB_SHARE)` of screens
over 2022–2025 went to running backs.

## How defenses fight back

None of this is free for the offense, because defenses coach against every one of these plays. The answers
belong to the defensive chapters, but here is the shape of each, so you can spot it on Sunday.

- **Against the fake:** linebackers are taught to read *through* their key. A guard who fires out but stops at
  the line, or a guard pulling the "wrong" way, says pass or boot even when the back says run; some teams have
  their linebackers *cross-key*, each watching the guard on the far side as well as his own. On obvious
  passing downs, many simply give ground first and react to the run late. ([Linebackers](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd)
  builds this.)
- **Against the boot:** the backside end is assigned to stay home (his checklist is *boot, counter, reverse*),
  and the flat defender on the boot side sinks under the over route instead of jumping the flat. Coverages with a
  middle-of-the-field [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber) or match rules that pass the crosser from one defender to the next take away the
  boot's middle read. ([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)
  and [Man Coverage](../06-pass-coverage/06-02-man-coverage.qmd).)
- **Against the screen:** a defensive lineman who feels his blocker let go is taught to stop rushing and turn to
  find the back ("smell" it), and a rusher who sees a back slip out can peel off and chase him. Defenses that
  expect a screen on third-and-long call a coverage that keeps an underneath defender home rather than blitzing.
  ([Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd).)

Each of those answers costs the defense something on another play: an end who stays home is not chasing the run,
and a lineman who stops to smell the screen is not rushing the passer. The offense's reply to the reply is the
subject of [Constraint Theory](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd).

## A short history

**Play-action** is as old as the legal forward pass (1906): as soon as a team could throw, faking a run
first was the obvious way to make a defense hesitate.[^forward] What changed over the twentieth century was
how *systematically* offenses built it in. The Wing-T of the 1950s made the run fake and the bootleg (its
waggle) part of a series in which every play looked like the others, the idea you met in
[03-05](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd).

The modern NFL bootleg game runs through **Mike Shanahan** and **Gary Kubiak** in Denver. Kubiak was the
Broncos' offensive coordinator from 1995 through 2005 under Shanahan, alongside Alex Gibbs's outside zone run
game of [03-02](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd), and John Elway, in the last four seasons of his
career, made faking outside zone and rolling away from it a staple. The pairing became a coaching tree's signature. Kyle Shanahan, Mike's son, was the Atlanta Falcons'
offensive coordinator in 2016, when Matt Ryan, throwing off play-action and boots, was named the league's
MVP. Kyle took the system to San Francisco as head coach in 2017, and Sean McVay and Matt LaFleur, who had
coached on his offensive staffs in Washington (and, for LaFleur, Atlanta), carried it to the Rams and the
Packers.[^tree]

Then the data caught up with the coaches. In 2018 Sean McVay's Rams went 13–3 and reached the Super Bowl
with Jared Goff throwing off play-action more than any quarterback in the league, on about 35 percent of his
dropbacks.[^rams18] In the same year Baldwin and Hermsmeyer published the analyses described above, showing
that play-action's value did not depend on the run game. The league was already moving that way: by Football
Outsiders' count, play-action rose from 18 percent of dropbacks in 2016 to 24 percent in 2018.[^parate] (Other
charting services count fakes differently, so their percentages are not comparable year to year.) In FTN's charting the league used play-action on `{python} pct(PA_RATE.loc[2022])` of dropbacks in
2022 and `{python} pct(PA_RATE.loc[2025])` in 2025, with the return of the under-center formation (see
[Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd)) helping push it up.

**Screens** are just as old, and no one owns them. The screen game most associated with the modern NFL is
**Andy Reid**'s. Reid learned the West Coast offense under Mike Holmgren in Green Bay, and from his first
years as a head coach in Philadelphia (from 1999) his teams threw running back screens as a core play, not a
gimmick, with Brian Westbrook as their best-known weapon in the 2000s. He took the same habits to Kansas City
in 2013.[^reid]

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Los Angeles Rams 2018"}
**The season:** the one in the history above. Notice the formation: the Rams faked nearly always from the same
11-personnel, tight-split sets they used for their outside zone runs with Todd Gurley (see the film room in
[Spread and Modern Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)). The "run
look" was not two tight ends; it was whatever the Rams ran from.

**What to notice:**

- The *match*. Line steps, back's path and receivers' splits are identical on the run and the fake. Try to
  call run or pass from the first step; you will be wrong often, and so were linebackers.
- The *crossers*. A large share of the big plays are receivers running across the field at 10–15 yards,
  behind linebackers who stepped up: the window of @fig-lb-void.
- The *boots*. Goff rolling away from outside zone with the flat, crosser and over routes, often after
  pre-snap motion has moved a receiver to the boot side.
- What went wrong in the Super Bowl: the Rams scored three points. New England packed the middle of the field,
  where the crossers run, and pressured Goff on about 43 percent of his dropbacks, much of it with stunts that
  had time to develop because Goff was holding the ball.[^sb53] A play-action game still needs time and room to throw.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Seattle Seahawks 2025"}
**The season:** Klint Kubiak's one year as Seattle's offensive coordinator, with Sam Darnold at
quarterback, ending in a 29–13 win over New England in Super Bowl LX.[^lx] Kubiak is Gary Kubiak's son, and
his offense was the Denver tree in its 2025 form: outside zone from tight formations and the boots and
play-action that pair with it. In FTN's charting, Seattle's play-action dropbacks averaged
`{python} f"{team25.loc['SEA', 'epa_pa']:+.2f}"` EPA, against `{python} f"{team25.loc['SEA', 'epa_no']:+.2f}"`
on its other dropbacks, `{python} "the biggest gap in the league" if TOP_GAIN == "SEA" else "one of the biggest gaps in the league"`
(@fig-pa-teams).

**What to do:** watch any Seahawks game from 2025 and keep two counts: how many dropbacks start with a run
fake, and how many of those move the quarterback out of the pocket. Then watch the linebackers on each fake
with this chapter's checklist. Kubiak was hired as the Raiders' head coach for 2026, so this was one season's
offense, not Seattle's current one.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Kansas City Chiefs 2022–2025, the screen game"}
**The record:** in FTN's charting, the Chiefs threw `{python} int(kc.loc['KC', 'n'])` screens over the four
seasons, `{python} "more than any other team" if kc.index[0] == "KC" else "among the most in the league"`,
and averaged `{python} f"{kc.loc['KC', 'epa']:+.2f}"` EPA on them, when the league average screen was worth
`{python} f"{LG_SCREEN_EPA:+.2f}"`. Most teams use screens as a tax on pressure; Reid's offense gets value
from them.

**What to notice:**

- The *sell*. Watch the Chiefs' linemen on a running back screen: they pass-set, punch and give ground as if
  in a real protection before releasing. A lazy release is the most common way screens die, and Kansas City's
  rarely look lazy.
- The *variety*. Running back slow screens, tunnel screens to receivers, tight end screens, screens off
  play-action and screens after motion: the defense cannot simply key one look.
- The *timing against pressure*. Watch what the Chiefs call on downs when an opponent has been blitzing;
  the screen is often the punishment.
:::

## The numbers: who fakes, and does it work?

Now the league-wide picture. In 2025 offenses used play-action on `{python} pct(PA_RATE.loc[2025])` of
dropbacks, and those dropbacks averaged `{python} f"{PA_EPA25:+.2f}"` EPA, against
`{python} f"{NO_EPA25:+.2f}"` for dropbacks without a fake; their success rate was
`{python} pct(PA_SR25)` against `{python} pct(NO_SR25)`. @fig-pa-teams breaks that down by team.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pa-teams
#| fig-cap: "Play-action by team, 2025 regular season. Each row is a team: EPA per dropback without a run fake (orange) and with one (blue); the line between them is the boost the fake gave that team. The right-hand column is the team's play-action rate (share of its dropbacks that began with a fake). Teams are sorted by that rate; where a team shows one dot (KC), the two sit on top of each other: the fake made no difference. Data: nflverse play-by-play with FTN charting via nflreadpy; dropbacks include sacks and scrambles."
t = team25.sort_values("rate")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.4, 5.6))
y = np.arange(len(t))
ax.axvline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=1, zorder=1)
ax.hlines(y, t["epa_no"], t["epa_pa"], color=style.GRID, lw=2.4, zorder=2)
ax.scatter(t["epa_no"], y, s=30, color=style.SERIES[1], zorder=3, label="No run fake", edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
ax.scatter(t["epa_pa"], y, s=30, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=4, label="Play-action", edgecolor=style.SURFACE, lw=0.6)
ax.set_yticks(y, t.index, fontsize=6.4)
ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=7.5)
xmax = float(max(t["epa_pa"].max(), t["epa_no"].max())) + 0.07
ax.set_xlim(float(min(t["epa_pa"].min(), t["epa_no"].min())) - 0.05, xmax + 0.12)
for yi, (rate, team) in enumerate(zip(t["rate"], t.index)):
    ax.text(xmax + 0.1, yi, f"{100 * rate:.0f}%", fontsize=6.4, color=style.INK_2, va="center", ha="right")
ax.text(xmax + 0.1, len(t) - 0.2, "PA rate", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, va="bottom", ha="right",
        fontweight="bold")
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(t) + 0.4)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.set_xlabel("EPA per dropback", fontsize=8, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_ylim(-0.8, len(t) + 1.6)
ax.legend(loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.42, 1.0), ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
ax.set_title("Most offenses are better when they fake", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three things stand out in @fig-pa-teams.

**Most teams were better with the fake.** `{python} N_BETTER25` of 32 offenses averaged more EPA on
play-action dropbacks than on their others. That is a single season, and some teams' play-action samples
are only a hundred-odd plays, so individual gaps bounce around from year to year. The league-wide pattern
does not.

**The heaviest users build their passing game on their run game.** McVay's Rams led the league at
`{python} pct(team25.loc['LA', 'rate'])` and Ben Johnson's Bears were next at `{python} pct(team25.loc['CHI', 'rate'])`.
Several other offenses from the Shanahan family tree sat in the top half (McDaniel's Dolphins, LaFleur's
Packers, Kubiak's Seahawks), though Shanahan's own 49ers ranked only `{python} ordinal(int(RANK['SF']))` in
2025. These are offenses whose runs and passes are designed to look alike before and just after the snap.

**Some offenses barely fake, and not all of them suffer for it.** The lowest rates belong to offenses built
around a shotgun quarterback who wins from the pocket, where a fake looks less like a run. The Chiefs ranked
`{python} ordinal(int(RANK['KC']))` in play-action rate but `{python} ordinal(int(EPA_RANK['KC']))` in EPA per
dropback, above the league's middle. Low use is a style, not a mistake: a fake is worth most when it looks like
your real run, and some offenses' real runs are not the ones defenses fear.

Why doesn't everyone fake on every snap, if it is worth that much? Because a fake only works while the defense
must respect the run (part of the measured boost belongs to the friendly early-down situations offenses pick for
it). On third-and-9, nobody bites.

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the linebackers' feet"}
**Before the snap**

- **Under center?** About four of every five under-center dropbacks begin with a run fake. When the
  quarterback lines up under the center, think run *or* play-action, not dropback.
- **The run look.** Whatever formation this offense runs its main run from (often 12 personnel, or 11 personnel
  with the receivers in tight splits) is the formation it fakes from.
- **The down and distance.** First-and-10 and second-and-short are play-action downs; third-and-long is not.

**At the snap: watch the linebackers' feet, not the ball**

- Did they step *forward*? Count the steps. Two steps up on a fake is a win for the offense. The main broadcast
  shot is usually framed on the box, so the linebackers are in it; the replay from the end zone, behind the
  offense, shows their first steps best.
- Did the guard in front of them fire out low, or pop up? If he popped up and they stayed home, the fake did
  not work, and the throw will be harder.

**In the first two seconds**

- Did the quarterback turn his back to the defense (under-center fake) or ride the back (shotgun)?
- Did he roll away from the fake? Find the backside end: did he chase (the boot wins) or stay home (watch for
  the quick throw to the flat, or a protected boot with a pulling guard or a back coming across)?
- **Only two receivers out, eight in to block?** Count the receivers who release. Two out with a hard fake on an
  early down is a shot play: look deep, at the single safety.
- **A tight end who blocks on the run-fake side, then slips out late** while everyone else floods the other way:
  that's the leak.
- **Linemen leaving their rushers and sliding out to one side before the throw?** It's a screen. Which ones released, and to which side? Did
  the rushers run past the back?

**After the play (on the replay)**

- How many yards did the crosser gain *after* the catch? That is the space the linebackers left.
- On a screen, count the blockers in front of the catch and the rushers behind it.

**For your prediction log** ([How to Watch a Broadcast](../01-foundations/01-06-how-to-watch-a-broadcast.qmd)):
on every under-center snap, write *run*, *PA* or *boot* before the snap. Then, when the defense blitzes on a
passing down, write *screen?* and see how often you are right.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 1: shot or not?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-shot
#| fig-cap: "Two snaps from the same game, both second-and-2 near midfield, both from the I formation (21 personnel) that the offense has handed off from on almost every early down today. Only the defense differs. Left (A): the defense has walked a safety down beside the tight end and left one safety deep in the middle. Right (B): both safeties stay deep and seven defenders are near the box. (The wide receivers and cornerbacks are just outside the picture.)"
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
for ax, single in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    if single:
        dfn = [q.moved(d=1.4, w=8.0) if q.key == "SS" else (q.moved(d=4.3, w=5.2) if q.key == "SAM" else q)
               for q in even_front(cb_w=13.5, shell="one")]
    else:
        dfn = [q.moved(d=12.5, w=-9.0 if q.key == "FS" else 9.0) if q.key in ("FS", "SS") else q
               for q in even_front(cb_w=13.5, shell="two")]
    dfn = [q.moved(w=-14.5) if q.key == "LCB" else (q.moved(w=14.5) if q.key == "RCB" else q) for q in dfn]
    p = Play(i_form(), dfn, los=50, to_go=2)
    draw(p, ax=ax, lateral=(-11.6, 11.6), window=(-8.6, 15.4))
    panel_title(ax, "A" if single else "B")
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Against which picture would you call the play-action shot, which defender is it aimed at, and what would
you call against the other one?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The shot goes against A, aimed at the one deep safety.** Count the defense. In A, eight players are within a
few yards of the line, so only three are deep enough to matter on a deep pass: two cornerbacks and the free
safety. The corners each have a receiver; the free safety is the only player protecting the middle of the field
deep, and the fake is aimed at *him*. If he takes two steps forward when the back hits the line, a deep post goes
over his head; pair the post with a deep over route from the other side (the yankee idea in @fig-shot-play) and he
cannot cover both. The down makes it cheap: on second-and-2, an incompletion leaves third-and-2, still a
comfortable down, and the defense *expects* a run here because this offense, like most
([01-02](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)), usually runs on second-and-short.

**Against B, don't take the shot.** Two safeties deep means two players over the top of the post and the over,
and the fake has to fool both. But B has paid for its deep help with only seven near the box, against seven
blockers (five linemen, the tight end and the fullback) with the back carrying the ball. Run the ball, or throw play-action to the *first* window: crossers behind linebackers who step up,
underneath the two deep safeties.

Notice what the clue was. Not the run game's yardage: the formation the offense always runs from, and how many
defenders the defense moved down to stop it.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 2: the end who won't bite"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-boot
#| fig-cap: "Same two-tight-end look the offense has run outside zone right from all game. On each of its last two naked bootlegs left, the backside end (ringed) did not chase the run fake: he stepped upfield and outside and waited for the quarterback (dashed orange), and both times the quarterback had to throw the ball away. It is first-and-10."
p = Play(ace_tight(), even_front(cb_w=10.0), los=30, to_go=10)
p.highlight("BE", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK)
fld = draw(p, lateral=(-14.5, 13.5), window=(-9.5, 13.0))
branch(fld, p, [(1.0, -4.0), (-0.6, -5.6), (-4.8, -6.8)], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.5)
say(fld, p, -7.6, -10.4, "what the end did\non the last two boots", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=7)
plt.show()
```

**What has the end taken away, what has he given up, and what are two good calls from this look?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**He has taken away the naked boot and given up some of his run defense.** He is playing his textbook rule:
the backside end on outside zone is taught to check **boot, counter, reverse** before he chases
([Perimeter Runs and Misdirection](../03-the-run-game/03-05-perimeter-and-misdirection.qmd)). An end who stays home
and waits for the quarterback is the one defender the naked bootleg cannot survive (@fig-naked-boot, right).

What he has given up depends on one thing: **he cannot tell the boot from the run until it is too late**, because
for the first second they look the same (that is the point of the boot). So if he has decided to stay home on the
boot, he is staying home on the run too, and he is no longer chasing the outside zone run from behind. The
backside of the run, where the back cuts back, is softer than it was.

**Two good calls:**

1. **Outside zone right**, and let the back cut back. The end's new habit has taken him out of the play's backside
   pursuit. (Or [split zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-zone), from
   [03-02](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd): a tight end or H comes across behind the line and kicks out
   the end, who is now sitting still and easy to find.)
2. **A protected bootleg** (@fig-boot-family, left): the same fake and the same boot, but a guard pulls, or a tight
   end or fullback comes across, to kick the end out. The end is now a blocked defender, and the quarterback gets the
   edge he wanted. The risk is the tell of a blocker going the "wrong" way, which is why it is a call to make after
   the defense has adjusted, not before.

And if the end still wins on a boot, the quarterback has a legal escape: once he is outside the tackles he may throw
the ball away with no receiver near it, as long as it reaches the line of scrimmage, without being called for
intentional grounding (the rule is in the screens section's note and in
[Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)). That is why "throw it away" was the right answer on the last two
boots, not a sack.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play 3: screen or not?"}
```{python}
#| label: fig-predict-screen
#| fig-cap: "Third-and-7, shotgun, 11 personnel; two different snaps, each frozen 1.2 seconds after the snap. The faint lines show where every player has come from (offense blue, defense orange). One of them is a screen."
T_P3 = 1.2


def te_screen(p):
    """Tight end screen right: the line sets, the RG and RT release outward, the Y blocks a count and slides out."""
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.3, 0.0)])
    go_to(p, "RG", (0.5, 3.6), "block", via=[(-1.6, 1.8)], speed=2.4)
    go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 7.0), "block", via=[(-1.6, 3.4)], speed=2.4)
    go_to(p, "Y", (-1.0, 5.2), "block", speed=0.8)
    go_to(p, "Y", (-2.4, 8.4), "route", delay=0.2, speed=3.5)
    go_to(p, "Y", (9.0, 10.4), "run", delay=0.1, via=[(1.0, 9.6)])
    go_to(p, "Z", (14.0, 14.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "X", (14.0, -15.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "H", (12.0, -9.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "QB", (-8.8, -0.4), speed=2.2)
    go_to(p, "RB", (-4.6, -3.2), speed=2.0)
    for k, end in (("SDE", (-5.4, 2.6)), ("SDT", (-5.0, 1.0)), ("WDE", (-1.8, -5.2)), ("WDT", (-0.6, -1.4))):
        go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.4)
    return p


def swing_left(p):
    """A swing to the back: the whole line pass-blocks and the back leaves at the snap."""
    pass_set(p)
    p.dropback(1.6)
    p.route("RB", r.swing(9.0), side=-1)
    go_to(p, "H", (14.0, -9.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "X", (16.0, -15.5), "route")
    go_to(p, "Y", (12.0, 9.0), "route")
    go_to(p, "Z", (14.0, 15.0), "route")
    for k, end in (("SDE", (-1.8, 5.2)), ("SDT", (-0.6, 1.6)), ("WDE", (-1.8, -5.2)), ("WDT", (-0.6, -1.4))):
        go_to(p, k, end, "rush", speed=3.4)
    return p


fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.6, 4.0))
for ax, build, name in zip(axes, (te_screen, swing_left), ("A", "B")):
    p = build(Play(spread(y_inline=(name == "A")), nickel(), los=40, to_go=7))
    moment(ax, p, T_P3, lateral=(-12.6, 12.6), window=(-10.5, 9.5), mark_r=0.8)
    panel_title(ax, name)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=0.6)
plt.show()
```

**Which snap is the screen, and to whom? What is the other one, and what told you?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A is a tight end screen to the right; B is a swing route to the back.** Look at the line first, not the ball.

- **In A, two linemen have left their rushers.** The right guard and right tackle set, gave a punch and are now
  sliding *out* to the right, level with the line, while the end and tackle they were blocking run free toward the
  quarterback. Linemen leave rushers on purpose only for a screen (or a run), and the side they slide to is the screen
  side. The Y, who blocked the end for a count, is slipping out behind them. The quarterback is drifting back to pull
  the rush deeper. The linemen are still level with the line because the ball has not been thrown yet: in the NFL
  they may not be more than a yard downfield until it is (the rule from earlier in the chapter).
- **In B, all five linemen are still pass-blocking**, and the back left at the snap and is already bowing out toward
  the left sideline on his own. Nobody is releasing in front of him. That is a route: a swing, an outlet the
  quarterback can throw whenever he wants.

The timing tells you less than you might think: a swing can be thrown at once or late as a checkdown. The line, and
whether the back *waited* before leaving, tell you every time.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Play-action works on the linebackers' run-fit triggers.** Defenders near the line must react to run
  signals fast; a fake that shows those signals (low line steps, the back's path, the handoff) moves them
  forward and opens the space behind them. It buys space, not protection.
- **It does not need a good run game.** Baldwin's 2018 analysis and this chapter's 2022–2025 rerun agree: a
  team's rushing efficiency barely predicts its play-action boost. What matters is that the fake **looks exactly
  like the real run**. Under-center play-action, the most convincing fake, was the most productive dropback in
  football over 2022–2025.
- The fake sends the ball to **three windows**: behind the linebackers (crossers, most of the value, much of it
  after the catch), behind the safeties (the **shot play**, with extra blockers and two or three receivers), and
  to the side the defense left (the **bootleg**).
- The **bootleg** moves the launch point away from the defense's flow, with three receivers at three depths. The
  **naked** boot bets that the end chases; the **keeper**, the **protected boot** and the **leak** answer the
  defense's adjustments to it.
- A **screen** invites the rush, releases linemen in front of a receiver behind the line (in the NFL they slide
  out along the line and turn upfield only after the throw) and throws over the rushers. **Slow, tunnel, jailbreak, tight end and middle** screens
  vary who catches it and where the blockers go. A **swing** or **flare** is a route, not a screen: nobody
  releases to block.
- **Screens punish pressure.** Their value climbs with every extra rusher; against a soft rush they are among the
  worst plays in football. They are a tax that keeps defenses from blitzing freely.

- [Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd): plays that are a run and a pass at once, and the one-yard rule that limits
  them; an RPO is not a fake but a real choice made after the snap.
- [Linebackers](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-04-linebackers-and-second-level.qmd) and
  [Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd): the keys and
  run-fit triggers this chapter glossed, from the defense's side, and how defenses teach linebackers to survive
  play-action.
- [Blitz and Man Pressure](../07-pressure/07-02-blitz-and-man-pressure.qmd): the pressures screens punish.
- [Constraint Theory and Sequencing](../08-the-chess-match/08-02-constraint-theory-and-sequencing.qmd): how
  play-action, boots and screens keep the base plays honest, and how play-callers sequence them.

**See also (case study):** [The Shanahan Tree: Wide Zone, Boots, and the Illusion of Complexity](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd)
and [Andy Reid's Chiefs](../12-case-studies/12-04-reid-chiefs.qmd).

**If you want to go deeper:** Ben Baldwin's and Josh Hermsmeyer's 2018 play-action analyses (footnoted
below) and Baldwin's later open-source work at Open Source Football; Chris B. Brown's *The Art of Smart Football*
on the bootleg and the screen game; and any Shanahan-tree offense's All-22 film, watched with nothing but the
linebackers' first two steps in mind.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From diagrams to real tracking data.** The animations in this chapter are gridiron simulations in NFL Big Data
Bowl (BDB) coordinates, the format of the league's public tracking-data competition. The 2025 Big Data Bowl release
(2022 season, weeks 1–9) records every player ten times a second, and its `plays.csv` marks each play's
`playAction` and `dropbackType`, so you can find real bootlegs and watch the linebackers step up on the fake. The
data needs a free Kaggle login, so this code is not run when the book is built.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real Big Data Bowl tracking; not run in the build)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
# play-action passes on which the quarterback rolled out by design (a bootleg or a rollout)
boots = plays[(plays["playAction"] == True)
              & plays["dropbackType"].astype(str).str.contains("ROLLOUT", case=False)]
print(len(boots), "play-action rollouts")
g, pl = boots.iloc[0][["gameId", "playId"]]

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.7, 1.5, 2.3])   # snap, the fake, the boot, the throw
```
:::

[^ineligible]: NFL Football Operations, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 8, Section 3, Article 1 ("Ineligible
    Player Downfield"): "On a scrimmage play during which a legal forward pass is thrown, it is a foul if the entire
    body of an ineligible offensive player ... is more than one yard beyond the line of scrimmage before the pass has
    been thrown"; a lineman blocking an opponent who started within a yard of the line may be carried past it, and
    Article 2 lets linemen advance once the ball is thrown. Penalty: five yards.
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>. The rule is taught in [Run-Pass Options](04-06-rpos.qmd).

[^baldwin]: Ben Baldwin, "Rushing Success and Play-Action Passing," guest column, Football Outsiders, February
    2018 (play-by-play charting, 2011–2017; the date and findings are summarized in Acme Packing Company, Aug. 3,
    2018: <https://www.acmepackingcompany.com/by-the-numbers/2018/8/3/17644926/packers-hoping-to-restore-the-declining-play-action-pass-in-2018>).
    Josh Hermsmeyer, "Can NFL Coaches Overuse Play-Action? They Haven't Yet," FiveThirtyEight, 2018:
    <https://fivethirtyeight.com/features/can-nfl-coaches-overuse-play-action-they-havent-yet/>; his tracking-data
    finding on middle linebackers is summarized in Ed Feng, "How Super Bowl contenders use analytics," The Power
    Rank, Sept. 10, 2021: <https://thepowerrank.com/2021/09/10/how-super-bowl-contenders-use-analytics/>. Baldwin
    and Sebastian Carl are the authors of nflfastR: <https://www.nflfastr.com/>. The same sources are used in
    [Expected Points, EPA, and Success Rate](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd).

[^ftn]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`load_pbp`) joined to FTN charting (`load_ftn_charting`,
    fields `is_play_action`, `is_screen_pass`, `qb_location`, `is_qb_out_of_pocket`, `n_pass_rushers`), 2022–2025
    regular seasons. A dropback is any play with `qb_dropback == 1`, including sacks and scrambles, spikes
    removed. Running back carries for the run-game measure are runs by players listed as RB or FB on nflverse
    rosters, excluding scrambles and kneels. FTN's public data dictionary defines the fields only as "play-action
    pass," "screen pass" and "quarterback moved out of pocket," so edge cases (a shotgun ride, a fake jet sweep)
    are the charters' judgment: read team rates as one charting service's calls. Data dictionary:
    <https://nflreadr.nflverse.com/articles/dictionary_ftn_charting.html>.

[^ftnsack]: Course calculation from nflverse play-by-play (`load_pbp`) joined to FTN charting
    (`load_ftn_charting`, field `is_play_action`) via nflreadpy: dropbacks (`qb_dropback == 1`, spikes removed) on
    first and second down, 2022–2025 regular seasons, with `sack == 1`. Across all downs the comparison flips (play-action `{python} f"{100 * SACK[True]:.1f}"`%, others
    `{python} f"{100 * SACK[False]:.1f}"`%), because the no-fake group contains almost every third-and-long, when
    defenses rush hardest.

[^ftn2]: Same data and method as the previous note, 2025 season. The under-center comeback in personnel and
    formation data: see [Classic Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-03-classic-formations.qmd).

[^ftn3]: Same data; pass attempts that were not sacks, 2022–2025. Air yards and yards after the catch are
    nflverse's `air_yards` and `yards_after_catch` (the latter only on completions).

[^bootname]: The football name has no documented coinage; the hidden-ball explanation is the standard one
    (Wikipedia, "Bootleg play": the quarterback "hides the ball from the defense by his thigh ... similar to the way
    bootleggers would hide whiskey in their trousers during Prohibition": <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bootleg_play>).
    The word itself is older, from smugglers hiding goods in the legs of their boots: Merriam-Webster, "bootleg":
    <https://www.merriam-webster.com/dictionary/bootleg>.

[^ineligible2]: NFL Rule 8-3-1 (see the earlier note) has no exception for passes caught behind the line; the
    college rule does: NCAA Rule 7-3-10, "No originally ineligible receiver shall be or have been more than three
    yards beyond the neutral zone until a legal forward pass that crosses the neutral zone has been thrown"
    (<https://www.sdcfoa.org/ncaa/rule-7-snapping-and-passing-the-ball/college-7-3-10>). An NFL example of the rule on
    a screen: a 2024 ineligible-downfield flag on a Dak Prescott screen to Rico Dowdle was picked up only after replay
    showed where the lineman was relative to the line (ProFootballTalk, Sept. 27, 2024:
    <https://www.nbcsports.com/nfl/profootballtalk/rumor-mill/news/nfl-officials-used-replay-assistance-to-pick-up-flag-for-ineligible-man-downfield-not-holding>).

[^grounding]: NFL Football Operations, *2026 Official Playing Rules*, Rule 8, Section 2, Article 1 (intentional
    grounding): a foul if a passer facing an imminent loss of yardage throws a forward pass that is not in the
    direction and vicinity of an originally eligible receiver; it is not called when a passer who is or has been
    outside the pocket area throws a pass that lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage (including out of bounds).
    <https://operations.nfl.com/the-rules/nfl-rulebook/>. The rule is taught in
    [Quarterback Play](04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) and owned by
    [Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball](../09-special-teams-and-the-rules-that-shape-strategy/09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball.qmd).

[^forward]: The forward pass became legal in American football in 1906, after the rules reforms of 1905–06:
    <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forward_pass>.

[^tree]: Gary Kubiak was Denver's offensive coordinator 1995–2005 (Pro Football Reference coaching page:
    <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/KubiGa0.htm>). Matt Ryan was the 2016 AP MVP with Kyle Shanahan
    as Atlanta's offensive coordinator (<https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2016/>;
    <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/ShanKy0.htm>). McVay (Washington assistant 2010–13 while
    Shanahan was offensive coordinator) and LaFleur (Washington quarterbacks coach 2010–13, Atlanta quarterbacks coach
    2015–16): <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/McVaSe0.htm>,
    <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/coaches/LaFlMa0.htm>. The tree is traced in
    [Zone Running](../03-the-run-game/03-02-zone-running.qmd) and the
    [12-03](../12-case-studies/12-03-shanahan-wide-zone-tree.qmd) case study.

[^rams18]: 2018 Rams record and Super Bowl LIII (lost 13–3 to New England): Pro Football Reference,
    <https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/ram/2018.htm>. Goff "used play-action on 34.6 percent of his
    dropbacks, the highest mark in the league by more than 4 percentage points, according to Pro Football Focus":
    Robert Mays, The Ringer, Feb. 1, 2019:
    <https://www.theringer.com/2019/02/01/nfl/rams-sean-mcvay-play-action-history-bill-walsh-mike-shanahan>.

[^parate]: Danny Kelly, The Ringer, Sept. 3, 2019, citing the *Football Outsiders Almanac*:

[^reid]: Reid was a Packers assistant under Holmgren 1992–98, Eagles head coach 1999–2012 and Chiefs head coach from

[^sb53]: Ben Linsey, "Patriots follow blueprint for beating Jared Goff and the Rams to perfection," PFF, Feb. 4,
